title: agent-dns/1 — from a domain name to its agents
pitch: agent-dns/1 is a vendor-neutral way for a domain to say where its agents are described — one DNS TXT record at _agent.<domain> pointing at the domain's agent/1 discovery document.

refusals.title: One record
refusals.body: A domain has exactly one v=agent1 record at _agent.<domain>. Two is refused as duplicate-records — ambiguity is refused, never resolved by picking the first. Records of other versions at the same name are ignored, so a future agent2 can coexist with this one.

refusals.title: One url, and nothing else in DNS
refusals.body: The record carries a version, a url, an optional org, and nothing else. No capabilities, no keys, no endpoints in DNS. DNS points; the document describes.

refusals.title: Same domain only
refusals.body: The url must be https and its host must be the domain or a subdomain of it. Version 1 carries no Public Suffix List, so it does not guess whether co.uk is a suffix; it refuses parents and siblings as well as strangers. The narrower rule costs nothing a publisher cannot fix by publishing under the domain the url names.

refusals.title: Four findings, never collapsed; null is never zero
refusals.body: A resolver reports ok, absent, unreachable or invalid and never anything else. unreachable is a fact about the resolver's connectivity, never evidence that a domain has no agent; only an actual answer of nothing — no record, or a 404/410 — reads absent.

refusals.title: Refuse, don't guess
refusals.body: A non-https url, a cross-host url, a missing v=agent1, a missing url, an unknown key without x-, a repeated key, or a domain that is not a hostname is each invalid with a stable reason code, and each has a vector.

faq.a: A non-https or cross-host url; a record missing v=agent1 or url; a key the contract does not name unless x- prefixed; a repeated key; more than one v=agent1 record; and a domain that is not a hostname. Each is invalid with a stable reason code, and each has a vector that names it.

faq.q: Where does this sit in Web 4?
faq.a: The gateway layer — 'how do I connect to the old web?'. DNS bootstrapped the web by turning a name into an address; agent-dns/1 does the same for the agentic internet — the name is the domain, the address is one https URL, and everything else lives in the agent/1 document it points at. The stack page and the Web 4 hub show where it sits among the nine layers.

No. agent-dns/1 is draft. Nothing here is deployed, adopted or measured; the vectors and tests are the whole of the evidence, and the grammar, algorithm and reason codes may change until the first independent implementation agrees with them.

faq.q: Why only one record and one url?
faq.a: Because ambiguity is refused, not resolved. Two v=agent1 records is duplicate-records; the record carries a version, a url and an optional org and nothing else. DNS points to exactly one document; the document describes everything else.

faq.q: Why refuse a parent or sibling domain?
faq.a: Because there is no Public Suffix List here and version 1 will not guess one. Host must equal the domain or be a subdomain of it — so acme.co.uk and other.co.uk are never read as one publisher. A rule stated by guessing is guessed wrong at least once.

faq.q: Does this repository touch the network?
faq.a: No. resolve() takes an injected lookupTxt and fetcher, and every test uses in-memory maps. The one snippet that wires node:dns/promises and fetch lives in the README and is labelled as not exercised by the tests.
